workspace.title: Choose a Database for the Orders Service

nodes.title: Which database should we use for the new orders service?
nodes.summary: We need to pick a primary database for the orders service before we start implementation. Key requirements: strong consistency for order state transitions, ability to handle 8k writes/min at peak, and operational sustainability for a team of four.

nodes.title: Use PostgreSQL on RDS
nodes.summary: Run PostgreSQL via Amazon RDS. The team already operates one RDS cluster for the user service, so runbooks and alerting are in place. ACID transactions give us the consistency guarantees we need for order state changes.

nodes.title: Does our existing RDS expertise cover the operational burden?
nodes.summary: We already run RDS for the user service. The same backup schedules, CloudWatch alarms, and failover runbooks apply. Concluded: yes, existing expertise transfers directly.
nodes.conclusion: Yes — existing RDS operational knowledge transfers directly to a second cluster.
nodes.rationale: Same managed service, same monitoring stack, same incident runbooks. No new skills required.

nodes.title: Write throughput must sustain 8k orders/min during flash sales
nodes.summary: Peak load is 8k orders/min (~133 writes/sec). A db.t3.large RDS instance benchmarks at ~500 writes/sec for simple inserts, so headroom appears sufficient — but this needs load testing before we commit.

nodes.title: Use MongoDB Atlas
nodes.summary: Run MongoDB via Atlas managed service. The document model could map naturally to order objects (nested line items, addresses, metadata). Atlas handles backups and scaling automatically.

nodes.title: Does the document model actually fit our order schema?
nodes.summary: Orders have nested line items and addresses that map naturally to documents. But we also need cross-order aggregations (revenue by SKU, refund rates) that are awkward without joins. Not yet resolved.

nodes.title: Multi-document ACID transactions are required for order state changes
nodes.summary: A single order state change touches the order record, inventory reservation, and a ledger entry. All three must succeed or fail together. MongoDB 4.x+ supports multi-document transactions but they come with a performance penalty that needs evaluation.

nodes.title: Use DynamoDB
nodes.summary: DynamoDB offers near-unlimited write throughput and zero operational overhead. However, it requires access patterns to be fixed upfront, and our analytics requirements are still evolving. Deferred until access patterns are stable.

nodes.title: Is AWS vendor lock-in acceptable given our multi-cloud strategy?
nodes.summary: DynamoDB is AWS-only. Our infrastructure strategy prefers portable components where cost is comparable. Deferred with the parent option.

nodes.title: All access patterns must be defined before schema design
nodes.summary: DynamoDB requires knowing your queries upfront to design the partition/sort key structure. Our analytics requirements are still changing week to week, making this premature.

messages.content: Let's think through the PostgreSQL option. What's the strongest case for it given our requirements?

The strongest case for PostgreSQL here is transactional integrity. Order state changes — placed → confirmed → shipped → refunded — touch multiple tables atomically. PostgreSQL's ACID guarantees handle this natively with standard `BEGIN / COMMIT` blocks, and you get row-level locking with `SELECT FOR UPDATE` for concurrent order updates without building your own optimistic concurrency layer.

On RDS specifically, you also get point-in-time recovery, automated minor version patches, and Multi-AZ standby for free, which would otherwise be your first month of work with a self-managed cluster.

The secondary benefit is that your team already knows this. You're not learning a new consistency model or data API — you're applying the same mental model you use on the user service.
What about write throughput? We peak at around 8k orders per minute during flash sales — roughly 133 writes per second. Will a typical RDS instance handle that?

133 writes/sec is well within range for a properly tuned RDS instance. A `db.t3.large` can sustain ~400–600 simple inserts per second; a `db.m6g.large` pushes that above 1,000. Your bottleneck is more likely connection count than raw throughput — RDS PostgreSQL struggles above ~200 concurrent connections, so you'll want a connection pooler (PgBouncer via RDS Proxy, or a sidecar) in front of it.

One caveat: if a single flash-sale order write touches the order row, inventory, and ledger in one transaction, your effective write rate triples (3 row writes per logical order). At 400 logical orders/sec that's 1,200 row writes, which is still fine for an m6g.large but worth modeling before you commit to an instance size.

I'd recommend running a load test at 2× your expected peak before launch. pgbench can simulate this against a staging instance in an afternoon.
